title: Type Conversion
description: Master implicit and explicit conversions, casting, parsing, TryParse, and the Convert class — with examples of overflow, truncation, and safe conversion patterns.

data.text: Real programs constantly move data between different types. You might read a number as text from a file, calculate a total as a `double` and need to round it to an `int`, or accept user input as a `string` and convert it to a `DateTime`. **Type conversion** is the mechanism C# uses to transform data from one type to another.

C# has two categories of numeric conversion: **implicit** (automatic, no data loss) and **explicit** (requires a cast, possible data loss). For converting between strings and other types, C# provides `Parse`, `TryParse`, and the `Convert` class.

data.text: An **implicit conversion** happens automatically when C# is certain no data loss will occur. This typically means converting from a smaller type to a larger type. The compiler does the work without any special syntax.

rows: short, int, long, float, double, decimal
ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, float, double, decimal

data.title: Implicit Conversions
data.content: Automatic widening conversions that never lose data

data.text: When converting from a larger type to a smaller one, C# requires an **explicit cast** using the `(type)` syntax. The compiler cannot guarantee that the value fits in the target type, so it demands that you acknowledge the risk.

data.title: Truncation and Overflow
data.text: Casting a floating-point number to an integer **truncates** (drops the decimal part, it does NOT round). Casting a number that exceeds the target type's range causes silent overflow (wrapping) in unchecked context, or an OverflowException in checked context.

data.title: Explicit Casts and Overflow
data.content: Narrowing conversions that can lose data

data.text: By default, integer arithmetic in C# is **unchecked** — overflow wraps around silently. You can change this behavior with the `checked` keyword, which causes an `OverflowException` to be thrown when overflow occurs. This is useful for financial or safety-critical code where silent corruption would be a serious bug.

data.title: checked vs unchecked:
items: You can also enable checked arithmetic for the entire project in the .csproj: `<CheckForOverflowUnderflow>true</CheckForOverflowUnderflow>`
checked only affects integer types — floating-point overflow produces Infinity or NaN instead

data.text: User input, file contents, and API responses almost always arrive as strings. C# provides methods to convert strings to other types. `Parse` throws an exception if the string isn't valid. `TryParse` returns `true` or `false` and outputs the result through an `out` parameter — it never throws.

data.title: Parse vs TryParse
data.content: Converting strings to numeric types safely

data.text: The `System.Convert` class provides static methods for converting between base types. It handles `null` gracefully (converting it to the default value for the target type) and supports many types including `ToBoolean`, `ToDateTime`, `ToDecimal`, and more.

data.title: Using the Convert Class
Prefer TryParse
data.text: Use `TryParse` for user input or any data that might be invalid. It's faster than catching exceptions, and exceptions should be reserved for truly exceptional conditions — not expected user mistakes.

data.title: Exercise: Build a Number Parser
data.description: Write a program that reads numbers from the user and performs safe conversions.
steps: Prompt the user to enter an integer with `Console.ReadLine()`
Use `int.TryParse` to safely convert the input
If successful, convert the integer to `double` and divide by 2 — print the result
If it fails, print an error message and ask again (use a loop)
After a successful parse, also parse the same value as `decimal` and print both double and decimal versions side by side
Add a third input: ask for a `bool` using `bool.TryParse` and print the result
data.expectedOutcome: A program that safely reads and converts user input using TryParse, handles invalid input gracefully, and demonstrates the difference between double and decimal representations.

items.question: What is the difference between Parse and Convert?
items.answer: `int.Parse("abc")` throws a `FormatException`. `Convert.ToInt32("abc")` also throws. But `Convert.ToInt32(null)` returns `0`, while `int.Parse(null)` throws a `ArgumentNullException`. `Convert` is more forgiving of null.

items.question: Does casting round the number?
items.answer: No. Casting from double/float to an integer type **truncates** — it drops the decimal portion. Use `Math.Round()` before casting if you need rounding.

items.question: What is narrowing vs widening conversion?
items.answer: Widening (implicit) converts from a smaller type to a larger one without data loss. Narrowing (explicit) converts from a larger type to a smaller one and may lose data, requiring an explicit cast.

items.question: When should I use checked?
items.answer: Use `checked` in financial calculations or anywhere that silent overflow would cause incorrect results. For general-purpose code where performance matters and overflow is unlikely, `unchecked` (the default) is fine.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Implicit conversions happen automatically when no data loss is possible
Explicit casts use `(type)` syntax and may truncate or overflow
Casting from double to int truncates — it does NOT round
Use `checked` to detect overflow at runtime
`TryParse` is the safest way to convert strings to numbers
`Convert` class handles null gracefully but still throws on invalid format
data.takeaway: Type conversion is everywhere in C#. Choose the right method: implicit for safe widening, explicit cast with awareness of truncation, and TryParse for user input.
